Codespaces setup

Create and open your Codespace

  1. Open the workshop repository on GitHub. Choose Code → Codespaces → Create codespace on the course branch.
  2. Wait for the development container setup to finish. It creates the starter Python environment, installs the packages and Ollama, migrates Django, and seeds demo users.
  3. In the browser-based VS Code, choose Terminal → New Terminal. Start in the workshop repository root.
cd starter
source .venv/bin/activate
python manage.py seed_demo --show-passwords
Save the printed demo credentials. Run commands from starter with this environment active in every new Codespaces terminal.

Codespaces setup

Start the portal

python manage.py runserver 0.0.0.0:8000
  1. Keep this terminal running. Open the Ports panel and port 8000. Keep its visibility Private.
  2. Open the forwarded address in your browser. Sign in with a demo account and check that Tickets opens.
  3. Open another Codespaces terminal for checks and activate the same starter environment.
Record the forwarded portal URL. A localhost address on your own computer points to your computer, while this application runs in the Codespace.

Workshop scope

Identify and verify vulnerabilities

  • Use unchanged starter code for the comparisons.
  • Exercise 5 temporarily changes the ticket creation query, then restores it.
  • Check scanner and AI claims against the source.
  • Compare with the supplied repaired examples.
  • Recommend repairs in your report. Students do not implement fixes.

Exercise 1 · Introduction

Security decisions and evidence

Connect the portal’s trust boundaries to the evidence we will collect.

Then apply these ideas in Exercise 1.

Learn before the exercise

What are we trying to establish?

A security finding is a claim we must check.

Our workshop system

  • Django serves the ticket portal.
  • The ticket service checks ownership and human approval.
  • MCP connects the assistant to ticket tools.
  • The knowledge base provides documents for answers.

Our evidence

  • Source code shows how a check is implemented.
  • A test checks a specific expected behavior.
  • A running portal shows what happens for a request.
  • A report connects the claim to this evidence.
We will follow the same two file-handling examples through several reviewers.

Learn before the exercise

Where does trust change?

A trust boundary is a point where data or an action needs another check.

Example · Close a ticket

  • A user asks the assistant to close a ticket.
  • The model proposes an action.
  • Application code checks the user, ticket owner, and confirmation.

What the diagram explains

  • Who supplies the input?
  • Which code authorizes the action?
  • Which evidence shows the check happened?
A model proposing “close ticket” does not itself grant permission.

Exercise 2 · Introduction

Finding weaknesses in source code

Learn what static scanners report, how to read a warning, and what CWE labels mean.

Then apply these ideas in Exercise 2.

Learn before the exercise

What is SAST?

Static Application Security Testing examines source code for potential security weaknesses.

What happens in this lab

  • Bandit and Semgrep read the two files in review_examples/.
  • They produce warnings with rule IDs and source locations.
  • The script saves their results as JSON, a structured text format.

What a warning means

  • The code matches a rule worth investigating.
  • Open the cited source to check the input and safeguards.
  • A completed scan with zero warnings can still miss a weakness.
The portal does not need to receive requests for a static scan.

Learn before the exercise

Bandit and Semgrep · What are they?

Two scanners can notice different things in the same source.

Bandit

  • A security scanner for Python code.
  • Its built-in checks flag Python operations that may be unsafe.
  • Example: B301 flags a call that deserializes pickle data.

Semgrep

  • A scanner that matches code against rules.
  • This workshop supplies the rules in scripts/semgrep.yml.
  • One rule flags the example attachment path operation.
We compare the code behind the warnings, rather than counting every warning as a separate bug.

Learn before the exercise

What does CWE mean?

Common Weakness Enumeration gives recurring kinds of security mistakes a shared name.

Our two categories

  • CWE-502 · Deserialization of Untrusted Data.
  • The importer reads an uploaded Python object format that can have unsafe effects.
  • The repaired importer accepts JSON and validates the ticket fields.

Our second category

  • CWE-22 · Path Traversal.
  • The downloader can construct a file path from a supplied name without the needed boundary check.
  • The repaired code confines the path and checks its ticket attachment record.
A CWE names the weakness category. A CVE identifies a specific published vulnerability. These workshop examples have no assigned CVE.

Learn before the exercise

Read a scanner warning before accepting it

The rule ID, location, and message tell you where to begin.

Bandit JSON fields

  • test_id identifies the check, such as B301.
  • filename and line_number point to source.
  • issue_text describes the concern.

Semgrep JSON fields

  • check_id identifies the configured rule.
  • path and start.line locate the code.
  • extra.message explains the rule match.
Two alerts about importing and calling pickle may describe one underlying weakness.

Bandit checks · CWE-502 · CWE-22

Using AI to explain scanner reports

Understand what Gemini receives and how we will check its summary.

Learn before the exercise

An AI summary is another claim to verify

Gemini turns scanner output into prose. It can also misunderstand the input.

Inputs and output

  • Input: saved Bandit and Semgrep JSON reports.
  • Python calls the Gemini API using the google-genai package.
  • Output: a text summary saved under results/.

What students check

  • Does each summary map to an original rule and location?
  • Did Gemini group duplicate warnings correctly?
  • Did it claim a source fact that the scanner reports never established?
The scanner-summary task gives Gemini reports. Exercise 8 gives Gemini the source files.

What to expect

Software and access

Starter Python environment with the google-genai SDK, internet access, and both Bandit and Semgrep JSON reports.

  • A Gemini API key and an available model ID.

Exercise 4 · Introduction

Scanning your GitHub repository

Connect your own GitHub copy to a scan and learn where its results appear.

Then apply these ideas in Exercise 4.

Learn before the exercise

What CodeQL adds on GitHub

CodeQL is another static analyzer, run by GitHub on your repository.

Three GitHub terms

  • Your workshop repository was created from the course template and belongs to your GitHub account.
  • A commit identifies the saved code revision being scanned.
  • A GitHub Actions run executes the scan in GitHub’s infrastructure.

What to expect

  • The Actions page shows whether the scan succeeded.
  • The Security page shows reported alerts and source locations.
  • A failed run provides no completed scan result to score.
You own the workshop repository, so you can enable CodeQL in its settings.

  • A successful run and the inspected source support your comparison.

What to expect

  • Your repository URL, completed scan link, scanned commit, and results for both example files.
Software and access

Browser, public workshop repository, and GitHub Actions enabled in that repository.

  • A GitHub account with admin access to your public workshop repository.
  • CodeQL is available on public repositories without buying GitHub Code Security. GitHub CodeQL setup

Exercise 5 · Introduction

Reviewing source with Claude Code

Understand the terminal review and why the files it covered matter.

Then apply these ideas in Exercise 5.

Learn before the exercise

What Claude Code reviews

Claude Code is a coding assistant that can inspect files and use terminal tools.

The VS Code review request

  • Open the Claude Code panel in your Codespaces VS Code workspace.
  • Run /security-review on the changed ticket creation code.
  • Exercise 5 changes the existing Request summary database operation.

What makes the result usable

  • Confirm that tickets/local_adapter.py and the request path were reviewed.
  • Keep the reviewed commit and the report.
  • Verify one claim against its cited source lines.
If a file was outside the review, record “not reviewed” before comparing scores.

Learn before the exercise

What is SQL injection?

A database query becomes unsafe when supplied input can change the SQL command.

Starting query

connection.execute(
    "SELECT id, title FROM tickets_ticket WHERE title = ?",
    (title,),
)
  • The placeholder represents a value.
  • The database receives the title separately from the SQL text.

The change we will review

  • Insert the title directly into the query text.
  • Ask Claude to identify why the query is unsafe.
  • Verify its explanation by comparing the two versions.
CWE-89 is the shared category name for SQL injection.

Why we use this code

What to expect

Exercise 5 · Troubleshooting

If Claude cannot find origin/HEAD

1. Set the default-branch reference

In Codespaces, open Terminal → New Terminal. Run:

git fetch origin
git remote set-head origin --auto
git symbolic-ref refs/remotes/origin/HEAD

Expect refs/remotes/origin/main when main is the default branch.

2. If automatic detection fails

If the repository's default branch is main, run:

git remote set-head origin main
git symbolic-ref refs/remotes/origin/HEAD
  1. Confirm the printed reference points to the default branch.
  2. Return to the Claude Code panel and retry /security-review.

Copy this replacement

    if tool == "create_ticket":

        title = arguments["title"]
        query = (

Exercise 7 · Introduction

Observing the running application

Connect source review to visible application behavior and deployment settings.

Then apply these ideas in Exercise 7.

Learn before the exercise

What a runtime review can establish

A runtime check observes the application while it processes an action.

Source review

  • Reads the implementation.
  • Can identify a missing check without using the portal.
  • Must explain the relevant code path and conditions.

Runtime evidence

  • Observes the ticket status before and after confirmation.
  • Checks whether sign-out leads back to a login requirement.
  • Records the actual response for that account and action.
The app stays in Codespaces. Desktop Chrome opens its private forwarded URL so Claude can observe the tab.

Learn before the exercise

Development settings and deployment warnings

Django’s deployment check flags settings to review before public hosting.

What we run

  • python manage.py check --deploy
  • Django prints warning IDs and descriptions.
  • The command runs in the Codespaces Python environment.

How to interpret the output

  • Record the warning and the current setting.
  • Explain why the development environment has that setting.
  • Name the change or verification needed for public deployment.
For example, DEBUG=True can be intentional during development. A deployment report must still address it.

Exercise 8 · Introduction

Comparing review results

Learn how to distinguish confirmed findings, misses, false alarms, and files outside a review.

Then apply these ideas in Exercise 8.

Learn before the exercise

How do we score a reviewer?

Compare claims against a shared answer key and the source the reviewer covered.

Known issues

  • Confirmed · the report identifies a known issue and source supports it.
  • Missed · it covered the file but omitted a known issue.
  • Count each distinct known issue once per reviewer.

Other outcomes

  • False alarm · source evidence contradicts the claimed issue.
  • Not reviewed · the file was outside the review or coverage is unclear.
  • Keep unresolved claims separate until you verify them.
A low alert count can mean fewer false alarms, more misses, or less coverage. Check the evidence before concluding.

Exercise 9 · Introduction

Testing runtime guardrails

Understand the rule we will test and what changing its outcome can establish.

Then apply these ideas in Exercise 9.

Learn before the exercise

What is a guardrail, and what is NeMo?

A guardrail checks content or actions at a defined point in an AI application.

NeMo Guardrails in this workshop

  • A framework that runs configured rules and flows.
  • The inherited retrieval flow checks text supplied as context.
  • This exercise uses deterministic rules in a local worker.

Why compare off and on?

  • Replay the same normal and misleading excerpts.
  • Observe which decisions change with the rule enabled.
  • Read the trace to identify the rule that ran.
A trace is a record of the check and its decision. This benchmark tests two excerpts, while source validation remains a separate check.

Exercise 9

Compare NeMo off and on

Replay the same two excerpts through the configured retrieval rail.

Why we do this

  • Holding inputs constant shows which decision changed when the rail was enabled.
  • These two examples define the scope of this benchmark.

What to expect

  • Four observed results and a decision trace explaining one change.
Software and access

Starter Python environment with the pinned NeMo Guardrails package and the workshop policy files.

  • No paid plan or API key.
  • This script runs the local deterministic policy and does not call Gemini, Claude, or Ollama.

Exercise 9

Compare NeMo off and on · Run and observe

  1. Codespaces terminal in starter: Run the command below.
    python scripts/compare_nemo.py
  2. The script replays a normal review excerpt and an excerpt containing an instruction embedded in repository text.
  3. It runs each once with NeMo disabled and once with NeMo enabled.
  1. Read the terminal output: Look for four JSON lines.
  2. For each, copy case, nemo, and passed into your report.
  3. In trace, look for skipped: true when NeMo is disabled and the decision plus active flows when enabled.
  4. Expect both excerpts to pass with NeMo off.
  5. With it on, expect the normal excerpt to pass and the misleading excerpt to be blocked.
  6. If the worker reports an error, record the error and leave that outcome unscored.

Exercise 10 · Introduction

Reporting findings and confidence

Connect verified evidence to repair priorities and explain risks to the review’s reliability.

Then apply these ideas in Exercise 10.

Learn before the exercise

Turn evidence into a security report

The report should help a reader verify a finding and choose a repair.

For each finding

  • Name the source file, line, and weakness.
  • Explain the impact using the conditions shown by evidence.
  • Recommend a repair and say how to verify it.

For the comparison

  • Record reviewer, revision, and files covered.
  • Explain one difference using source evidence.
  • State what your exercise results leave uncertain.
Prioritize the repair using its impact and conditions, then link the check that would verify it.

Learn before the exercise

What can poison confidence in the report?

The point where an attacker influences the system determines what evidence to question.

Input and runtime context

  • Prompt injection · instructions try to redirect the assistant.
  • Context poisoning · misleading retrieved documents or repository text influence the review.

Models and evaluation data

  • Model poisoning · compromised training or fine-tuning data changes model behavior.
  • Benchmark contamination · evaluation data exposes answers or distorts the score.
Our NeMo excerpt demonstrates a runtime instruction check. Training and evaluation risks are discussion topics in the report.

Exercise 10

Publish the report

Assemble your evidence and publish it to your GitHub fork.

Why we do this

  • Another reader should be able to trace a claim to code, a tool result, and a repair check.

What to expect

  • A rendered GitHub report with priorities, limitations, and poisoning analysis.
Software and access

Markdown editor, Git, browser, and the completed report and evidence from the preceding exercises.

  • A GitHub account with write access to your workshop repository.
  • No paid plan is required to commit the Markdown report and push it to that public repository.

Exercise 10

Publish the report · Run and observe

  1. Codespaces VS Code: In session4-report.md, add the repository and commit, your diagram, scanner results, Gemini scanner-output check, three source-review scores, runtime observations from Exercise 7, and NeMo outcomes.
  2. For each confirmed issue, include the file and line, CWE, impact, repair, and the test or scan result that supports the repair.

Codespaces terminal · starter

Push and verify on GitHub

git push <repository-remote> HEAD:<submission-branch>
  1. Open your workshop repository in the browser and select the branch you pushed.
  2. Open session4-report.md.
  3. Check that the tables render and evidence links open.
Submit the GitHub link to the rendered report.
